Feather-star robot moves through 3D space underwater with two actuators

NC State researchers use flexible wings for swimming, hovering and turning, demonstrating camera exploration and lifting while a wireless version remains future work.

NC State News ↗7 October 2026English editorial summary
StoryImages 1Videos 1

Structure does part of the work

NC State reported research published in Science Advances on October 7. Four flexible wings surround a central disk containing two actuators. Each wing returns to its original shape after bending. This mechanical design produces several motion patterns from a small number of inputs, reducing the need for a separate actuator for every direction.

Three modes enable maneuvering

Driving both actuators makes the wings pulse to raise the robot; slower flapping enables hovering and stopping lets it descend. Driving one actuator creates fish-like propulsion, while rapidly alternating the two produces rotation. The paper’s abstract reports a maximum swimming speed of 1.64 body lengths per second and a peak rotation rate of 90 degrees per second.

Demonstrations and remaining work

The researchers demonstrated underwater camera exploration and object lifting, both individually and with multiple robots. These experiments show platform capabilities rather than commercial performance at sea. A fully wireless version is a future direction, and the team is seeking collaboration with specialists in other fields to develop suitable applications.
